title: AI Agents Are Fundamentally Restructuring the Software Paradigm
content:
Computer Science > Software Engineering
  [Submitted on 4 Jun 2026 (v1), last revised 10 Jun 2026 (this version, v2)]
    Title:Agentic Software: How AI Agents Are Restructuring the Software Paradigm
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:For over half a century, software engineering has operated on a foundational premise: human engineers decompose problems, encode decision logic into static code, and manually adapt that code as requirements evolve. This paper argues that the emergence of AI agents -- systems where large language models serve as the primary reasoning engine, dynamically generating and discarding code as an instrumental resource -- constitutes a fundamental restructuring of what software is, not an incremental tool improvement. We formalize the distinction between traditional deterministic software and agentic software: in the former, code is the carrier of pre-written decision logic; in the latter, the agent itself is the software, and its decision logic is generated at runtime. We trace the historical arc from licensed software to SaaS to Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), showing that each shift transferred additional complexity away from end-users -- with the agentic shift transferring not just operational complexity but decision-making complexity itself. We introduce Agentic Engineering as an expansion of the software engineering discipline into a new paradigm, distinct in its core object of study (agent systems rather than static source code), its control model (LLM-driven rather than human-predefined), and its human role (intent architect rather than code author). Through analysis of recent benchmark evidence including SWE-bench Verified, EvoClaw, and LangChain's multi-agent coordination studies, we demonstrate both the transformative potential of the agentic paradigm and its current limitations. We conclude with a four-stage roadmap toward self-evolving agent ecosystems and concrete recommendations for practitioners navigating this transition.

report.summary: New arXiv paper argues AI agents fundamentally restructure software, shifting from static code to runtime-generated decision logic and a new agentic engineering paradigm.
report.background: For over 50 years, software engineering relied on human engineers manually encoding decision logic into static code and updating it as requirements changed. The rapid advancement of large language models has enabled agents that can reason, generate, and discard code dynamically, making the agent itself the software rather than code. This paper traces a historical arc from licensed software to SaaS to Agent-as-a-Service, showing how each shift moved complexity away from end-users. The agentic shift goes further by transferring decision-making complexity itself. Industry momentum is visible in benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and multi-agent coordination studies from LangChain, which highlight both the promise and current limitations of LLM-driven systems. The authors formalize Agentic Engineering as a new discipline with different objects, control models, and human roles.
key_points: The paper formalizes a core distinction: traditional deterministic software uses code as the carrier of pre-written logic, while agentic software treats the agent as the software, generating decision logic at runtime. This is not an incremental tool improvement but a fundamental shift in what software is.

It introduces Agentic Engineering as a new discipline focused on agent systems rather than static source code. Its control model is LLM-driven instead of human-predefined, and the human role evolves from code author to intent architect who guides outcomes rather than implementing every detail.

The paper places the shift in historical context, from licensed software to SaaS to Agent-as-a-Service. Each transition moved operational complexity away from users, but the agentic transition additionally moves decision-making complexity, representing a deeper change in how software solves problems.

Recent benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified, EvoClaw, and LangChain's multi-agent coordination studies show transformative potential but also clear limitations. The paper argues these results reveal a roadmap toward self-evolving agent ecosystems and provides practical recommendations for practitioners navigating this transition.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a move from building models to orchestrating adaptive agent systems, pushing investment toward agent evaluation, memory, and multi-agent coordination rather than raw model quality. Developers will need to shift from writing deterministic code to designing intent specifications, monitoring runtime behavior, and managing emergent outcomes. Regular users benefit from software that adapts and performs complex tasks with less explicit instruction, but they also face new risks around reliability, transparency, and accountability. The paper suggests that the core discipline of software engineering must expand to encompass agentic systems, changing testing, debugging, and deployment practices. This could accelerate AI adoption across industries while demanding new governance frameworks to ensure safety in autonomous decision-making.
report.tools: Interested readers should watch SWE-bench Verified as the standard for evaluating agentic coding performance, and EvoClaw for runtime agent adaptation studies. LangChain and LangGraph are widely used frameworks for building and coordinating multi-agent systems. Open-source projects such as AutoGPT and CrewAI offer practical entry points for experimenting with agentic software, while alphaXiv and arXivLabs provide useful tools for exploring and annotating AI research papers.
